summary:
Samara Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and no discrimination protection is available. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records these as the operative national conditions and counts 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.

The same Home Office note assesses that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely on the basis of their sexual orientation, while trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and people in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. That assessment applies to a trans visitor to Samara Oblast. The note records no division-specific facts, and no regional divergence for this division.

The extremist designation is enforced through convictions. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated International LGBT Movement or for displaying its symbols, of which 98 were administrative and 3 criminal. At least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024 onward.

Charges carry long sentences: three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years, and repeated display of banned symbols is punishable by up to four years in prison. Human Rights Watch states these national-level facts apply in Samara Oblast.
tangentialFactors:
The Home Office note's risk differentiation matters for expectations on the ground. Sexual orientation alone is not assessed as sufficient to establish general persecution risk in Russia, but trans identity and public advocacy are. A visibly transgender visitor therefore sits in the category the note treats as likely to face persecution, a sharper exposure than that faced by an LGB visitor who is not perceived as trans.

The split between administrative and criminal outcomes is significant for a visitor. Of the 101 convictions recorded by June 2025, 98 were administrative and 3 criminal, but at least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024 and the publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 face sentences of up to 12 years. Symbol display alone can escalate to a four-year prison term when repeated.
localsOnly:
Residents of Samara Oblast live under the same prohibitions as visitors: no legal route to change gender markers on official documents, no access to trans-specific healthcare since 2023, no statutory discrimination protection, and no recognition of same-sex marriage.

Russian citizens resident in the oblast are reachable by both administrative and criminal provisions of the extremism statutes, and repeat display of banned symbols carries up to four years of imprisonment, with the more serious publishing-related charges carrying up to 12 years.

The Home Office note is a UK asylum standard and does not confer protection on residents of Samara Oblast; it governs how UK authorities assess claims brought by people who have left Russia.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Samara Oblast-specific enforcement figures appear in the inventory. The conviction totals, criminal-charge counts and sentence ranges are national Russian figures which Human Rights Watch states apply in Samara Oblast, but whether any of those cases were brought in this oblast is not sourced here.

The Home Office note expressly records no division-specific facts for Samara Oblast, and no source in the inventory documents a regional divergence in how the national framework is applied here. Whether local authorities in the oblast act more or less aggressively than the national average remains unresolved.

The 139-person figure covering anti-LGBT+ law impacts between 2022 and 2024 is a nationwide total with no breakdown by oblast; its distribution across Samara Oblast is not sourced.
